title: THE FRIEND WHO HELPED DESTROY A PRINCESS: WHEN THE WRONG VOICE TURNS SECRET SIN INTO SOMEONE ELSE’S NIGHTMARE
paragraphs: THE FRIEND WHO HELPED DESTROY A PRINCESS: WHEN THE WRONG VOICE TURNS SECRET SIN INTO SOMEONE ELSE’S NIGHTMARE

Amnon had a wicked desire. Jonadab had a clever plan. Tamar paid a devastating price. And buried inside 2 Samuel 13 is a warning every parent, every young person, every believer, and every person who has ever trusted the wrong friend needs to hear.
“But Amnon had a friend.” — 2 Samuel 13:3 (KJV)
Six words.
Because sometimes the most dangerous person in your life is not the one who openly hates you.
Sometimes it is the person who sits beside you, laughs at your jokes, knows your secrets, understands your weaknesses, and knows exactly what to say when your conscience is trying to stop you.
His name was Jonadab.
He was not an invading enemy. He was not a stranger hiding outside the palace gates.
He was family.
He was a friend.
And when Amnon was wrestling with a desire that should never have been entertained, Jonadab did not tell him to repent.
He taught him how to arrange the opportunity.
What followed was not a harmless mistake. It was sexual violence, betrayal, humiliation, and a family tragedy whose consequences would echo through the house of David.
But before we walk into that terrible room, there is something we must understand.
Not everyone who helps you get what you want is helping you become who God created you to be.
Some people will help you satisfy a desire while remaining completely indifferent to the person that desire may destroy.
And the frightening part?
They may call themselves your friends.
The story begins in 2 Samuel 13.
Amnon was a son of King David. Tamar was his beautiful half-sister, the full sister of Absalom.
Scripture tells us Amnon became consumed with desire for Tamar. He was distressed, frustrated, and increasingly troubled because he could not have what he wanted.
The biblical narrator uses the language of love to describe Amnon's feelings, but what happens next exposes how profoundly corrupted those feelings had become.
Love does not require another person to surrender their dignity.
Love does not manipulate.
Love does not force.
Love does not destroy someone and then discard them.
What Amnon called love became an obsession that refused to recognize Tamar's humanity.
And that is where Jonadab entered the story.
The King James Version says:
“But Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab, the son of Shimeah David's brother: and Jonadab was a very subtil man.” — 2 Samuel 13:3
Notice how Scripture introduces him.
Not as an enemy.
Not as a criminal.
As a friend.
The Hebrew text describes Jonadab as אִישׁ חָכָם מְאֹד — ish chakham me'od, meaning a very wise, clever, or shrewd man.
The Hebrew word chakam (חָכָם) can describe wisdom or skill. But the context determines how that intelligence is being used.
Jonadab was clever.
He could read people.
He could recognize weakness.
He could develop a strategy.
But intelligence without righteousness can become a weapon.
A person can be brilliant at solving problems and still be dangerously foolish about what is right.
Jonadab noticed Amnon's condition.
He asked why the king's son looked so troubled morning after morning.
Amnon confessed his desire for Tamar.
Now imagine that moment.
Imagine what a godly friend could have said.
“Amnon, she is your sister. You need to stop feeding this desire.”
“Do not confuse your feelings with permission.”
“You are about to hurt someone who trusts this family.”
“Let me help you turn away before you destroy your life and hers.”
That would have been friendship.
That would have been courage.
That would have been love.
Instead, Jonadab offered a plan.
In 2 Samuel 13:5, he told Amnon to lie down, pretend to be sick, wait for King David to visit, and ask that Tamar be sent to prepare food in his presence.
Read that again.
Jonadab did not merely encourage a sinful thought.
He supplied the deception that would help Amnon isolate Tamar.
He understood the palace.
He understood the father's concern for his son.
He understood how Tamar's kindness and family duty could be exploited.
He took something innocent—a sister caring for a supposedly sick brother—and turned it into the setting for a terrible betrayal.
There is a chilling lesson here.
The wrong friend does not always create the evil in your heart. Sometimes the wrong friend simply gives it a plan.
And that is why Proverbs 13:20 matters:
“He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.” (KJV)
Friendship is never spiritually neutral.
The people closest to us can strengthen our conscience or teach us to silence it.
They can help us confess what is wrong or teach us how to conceal it.
They can point us toward Jesus or convince us that getting what we want matters more than obeying Him.
Think about your own life.
Who do you call when temptation becomes overwhelming?
Who hears the thoughts you are ashamed to admit publicly?
Who has access to the version of you that nobody else sees?
And when you confess something dangerous, do they help you resist it?
Or do they help you justify it?
Because the person who laughs while you compromise may not be the person who stands beside you when the consequences arrive.
Amnon followed Jonadab's counsel.
He pretended to be sick.
David visited him.
Amnon asked for Tamar.
And David sent her.
There is something especially painful about this part of the story.
Tamar was not sneaking into a forbidden place.
She was obeying a request from her father, the king.
She entered her brother's house to perform an act of care.
She prepared food.
She approached someone who claimed to need help.
And the trust that brought her into that room was used against her.
Amnon then ordered the others to leave and demanded that Tamar come closer.
When he seized her and demanded sex, Tamar resisted.
Her words in 2 Samuel 13:12 are devastating:
“Nay, my brother, do not force me; for no such thing ought to be done in Israel: do not thou this folly.” (KJV)
She said no.
She identified the act as wrong.
She pleaded with him.
She spoke about the disgrace and harm that would follow.
She tried to reason with a man who had already decided that his desire mattered more than her voice.
And Scripture tells us:
“Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her.” — 2 Samuel 13:14 (KJV)
Those words should never be softened.
Amnon raped Tamar.
She did not consent.
She did not cause it.
She did not deserve it.
Her kindness was not an invitation. Her presence was not permission. Her relationship to Amnon did not make the violation less serious.
And no amount of spiritual language should ever transfer the blame from the perpetrator to the person he harmed.
Tamar was sinned against.
Amnon was responsible for his actions.
Jonadab's counsel helped arrange the opportunity.
And the adults and family structures around Tamar failed to give her the protection and justice she needed.
Then came another cruelty.
After assaulting Tamar, Amnon's feelings turned to hatred.
The man who claimed to love her ordered her away.
The one who had demanded her presence now demanded her removal.
Tamar protested again, recognizing the additional harm of being cast out.
But Amnon refused to listen.
He called his servant and ordered Tamar out, and the door was bolted behind her.
Can you imagine that sound?
A door closing.
A bolt sliding into place.
And a young woman standing outside, carrying trauma she never chose.
Second Samuel 13:19 describes Tamar placing ashes on her head, tearing the distinctive robe she wore as a virgin daughter of the king, and going away crying aloud.
Her grief was visible.
Her devastation was public.
And yet the chapter does not record the justice or restoration she deserved.
Instead, verse 20 describes her living desolate in her brother Absalom's house.
The Hebrew word שֹׁמֵמָה — shomemah carries the sense of desolation or devastation.
Scripture does not invite us to treat Tamar as a disposable character in Amnon's story.
Her suffering matters.
Her voice matters.
Her future matters.
And if you have ever been betrayed by someone you trusted, hear this carefully:
What someone did to you does not define your worth before God.
You are not dirty because another person sinned against you.
You are not responsible for another person's violence.
You are not beyond God's compassion because your story contains something painful.
And you do not owe your abuser access, silence, or reconciliation without repentance, safety, and accountability.
Jesus Christ never asks us to rename evil as good.
He is full of grace and truth.
Both matter.
Perhaps one of the most heartbreaking details is that Tamar's suffering was not the end of the tragedy.
David became angry when he heard what had happened, but the chapter records no effective action from him against Amnon.
Absalom carried hatred toward Amnon.
Two years passed.
Then Absalom arranged Amnon's death.
The violence did not heal Tamar.
Revenge did not restore what had been taken.
And the royal family continued descending into conflict.
This is what unchecked sin can do.
It does not remain neatly confined to the person who first entertained it.
It spreads into relationships.
It damages families.
It produces grief that others must carry.
But we must be careful about one thing.
The lesson is not that every survivor's suffering inevitably produces further destruction.
Nor is it that Tamar somehow brought judgment upon her family.
The moral responsibility remains with those who chose evil, enabled it, or failed to confront it.
And Jonadab's role deserves serious attention.
Later in the chapter, when news of Amnon's death reached David, Jonadab appeared again.
He explained that Absalom had been determined to kill Amnon because of what Amnon had done to Tamar.
Jonadab knew the background of the tragedy.
The same man who had once supplied Amnon with a plan now spoke as someone who understood the consequences.
Scripture does not tell us everything Jonadab thought or felt.
It does not explicitly describe his private motives or record his repentance.
We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
But what Scripture does reveal is enough to warn us.
Jonadab's cleverness helped Amnon reach Tamar. It did not help Amnon become righteous.
And there is a difference between a friend who helps you escape discomfort and a friend who helps you escape sin.
One tells you what you want to hear.
The other loves you enough to tell you what you need to hear.
One protects your appetite.
The other cares about your soul and the people your choices may hurt.
One says, “Here is how you can get away with it.”
The other says, “You need to stop before somebody gets hurt.”
That second kind of friend may make you uncomfortable.
They may challenge your excuses.
They may refuse to participate in your deception.
They may insist that you seek help, confess wrongdoing, and accept accountability.
But Proverbs 27:6 says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” (KJV)
Sometimes the friend who refuses to help you sin is the friend who loves you most.
And sometimes the person who constantly agrees with you is not protecting your peace.
They are protecting your rebellion from being challenged.
There is also another warning hidden in this story.
Be careful whose suffering becomes invisible when you are discussing somebody else's desires.
People often talk about Amnon's lust.
They discuss Jonadab's manipulation.
They analyze David's failures.
They examine Absalom's revenge.
But Tamar must not disappear behind the men who shaped the tragedy.
She was not merely the consequence of their bad decisions.
She was a person with a voice, dignity, and a life.
And she was the one who pleaded for righteousness when the men around her failed to practice it.
That should convict the Church.
When somebody comes forward with an account of abuse, our first concern must not be how to protect the reputation of the powerful.
It must not be how to avoid embarrassment.
It must not be how to make the story disappear.
We must take harm seriously, protect those at risk, respond with compassion, and pursue appropriate accountability.
Romans 12:9 tells believers:
“Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.” (KJV)
We cannot claim to hate evil while protecting the systems that allow it to continue.
And we cannot call it biblical forgiveness when we pressure the wounded to remain silent.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending nothing happened.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
Repentance is not a public performance designed to avoid consequences.
True repentance turns away from sin and bears fruit consistent with that change.
Now here is where this ancient story becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps you have never known a Jonadab by that name.
But you may have known someone who told you to lie because the truth would cost too much.
Someone who encouraged you to pursue a married person because you deserved happiness.
Someone who laughed at your conscience when you were trying to leave pornography behind.
Someone who helped you hide an addiction, betray a spouse, manipulate a relationship, or exploit another person's trust.
Someone who kept saying, “Everybody does it.”
Or, “Nobody will ever know.”
Or, “You only live once.”
Or, “God will forgive you anyway.”
Listen carefully.
God's mercy is not permission to make plans for the sin you already know you should abandon.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic: God forbid.
Grace is not a hiding place for deliberate cruelty.
Grace is God's invitation to come out of darkness and walk in newness of life.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because if this story only teaches us to avoid bad friends, we have not yet reached the deepest need of the human heart.
We need more than better company.
We need a Savior.
We need the One who can expose what we have concealed, forgive what we have confessed, and transform the desires that have ruled us.
We need the One who does not use the vulnerable for His own gratification but gives Himself in sacrificial love.
The contrast is extraordinary.
Amnon used his strength to overpower someone weaker.
Jesus, though possessing all authority, humbled Himself and gave His life for sinners.
Amnon exploited another person's trust.
Jesus is faithful and true.
Amnon's distorted desire brought devastation.
Christ's self-giving love opens the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
In the Greek New Testament, Ephesians 5:2 says:
“καὶ περιπατεῖτε ἐν ἀγάπῃ” — kai peripateite en agapē.
“Walk in love.”
Paul then points to Christ, who loved us and gave Himself up for us.
The word ἀγάπῃ — agapē refers here to the love believers are commanded to practice, a love defined in this passage by Christ's sacrificial example.
That is not the love Amnon demonstrated.
Christlike love does not ask, “How much can I take from this person?”
It asks, “How can I honor God in the way I treat this person?”
It does not turn another human being into an object.
It recognizes that every person bears dignity as one made in God's image.
And for the person reading this who has committed serious wrong, the Gospel does not offer cheap excuses.
It calls you to repentance.
Stop blaming temptation.
Stop blaming the people you harmed.
Stop hiding behind religious language.
Confess the truth.
Turn from the behavior.
Accept appropriate consequences.
Seek qualified help where needed.
Make restitution where possible without pressuring the person you harmed.
And come to Jesus with genuine repentance.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise is glorious.
But it is not a license to continue abusing, deceiving, or exploiting others.
The grace that forgives also teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
And to the person carrying wounds from someone else's sin, the invitation is different.
You do not need to confess guilt for what was done against you.
You need compassion, safety, truth, and support.
You may need people who will listen without minimizing your experience.
You may need professional care and the protection of appropriate authorities.
And you may need time.
Healing is not a competition.
You do not have to pretend you are fine to prove that you trust God.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
That verse does not promise that every wound disappears immediately.
It reveals something precious about the character of God.
He does not despise the brokenhearted.
He draws near.
And this is where the message of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a slogan.
Not because every scandal ends happily on earth.
Not because every victim receives justice immediately.
Not because every family becomes whole again.
And certainly not because the past can be erased by pretending it never happened.
But because sin and suffering do not have the final authority over those who belong to Christ.
The cross declares that God takes evil seriously.
The resurrection declares that death and darkness will not have the final word.
And the Gospel declares that repentant sinners can be redeemed and wounded people are never beyond the reach of God's compassionate care.
Jesus does not rewrite history by denying what happened.
He changes our eternal future through His death and resurrection, and He calls us to walk in His truth today.
Perhaps the most important question now is not simply, “Who was Jonadab?”
It is this:
Who has been advising your heart lately?
Whose voice are you trusting when you are tempted?
Who tells you the truth when you are wrong?
And whose voice are you becoming in somebody else's life?
Are you helping a friend repent?
Or helping them conceal their sin?
Are you protecting the vulnerable?
Or protecting the reputation of the person who hurt them?
Are you using your intelligence to serve righteousness?
Or to make disobedience easier?
Because you may never stand in a royal palace.
You may never counsel a king's son.
But one day somebody may come to you carrying a dangerous desire, a secret compromise, or a decision that could wound another person.
And what you say next may matter more than you realize.
Do not be Jonadab.
Be the friend who tells the truth.
Be the parent who teaches children that love never excuses coercion.
Be the believer who protects those who are vulnerable.
Be the Christian who refuses to confuse loyalty with covering up evil.
Be the person who chooses righteousness even when righteousness costs you a friendship.
And if you recognize yourself in the person who has been taking the wrong advice, do not wait until another life is damaged before you change direction.
Turn to Christ today.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is hope for the broken.
There is a better way to live.
And there is a Savior whose truth is stronger than the lies we have learned to believe.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Have you ever had someone encourage you to do something you knew was wrong?
Or have you ever been the person who needed the courage to tell a friend, “No. I will not help you do this”?
And if you have experienced betrayal or abuse, please know that you do not owe anyone your story in a public comment. Your safety and dignity matter more than engagement on a post.
If this ministry has helped you grow, I also want to invite you to become part of what we are building.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing biblical truth, Gospel-centered encouragement, and discipleship resources with people who are hungry to know Christ more deeply.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and remain rooted in biblical truth.
But making resources available, developing new materials, and expanding the ministry takes time, effort, and financial support.
And God's grace, forgiveness, and blessing cannot be purchased.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through shared commitment to making the truth of Christ known.
These products can serve as reminders of faith and encouragement, but the heart of the ministry will always be Jesus Christ and His Word.
Now, before we close, let us pray.
Heavenly Father,
Search our hearts.
Show us the voices we have allowed to influence our decisions.
Forgive us for the times we have mistaken cleverness for wisdom, approval for friendship, and personal desire for love.
Give us courage to resist evil even when it is disguised as good advice.
Teach us to be friends who speak truth with humility and compassion.
Protect our children, our families, and the vulnerable among us from those who would exploit their trust.
Lord, we remember those who, like Tamar, have suffered betrayal, abuse, and injustice.
Draw near to them.
Surround them with people who will listen, believe them without rushing to judgment, take their safety seriously, and help them receive the support and justice they need.
Let no wounded person believe that another's sin has made them worthless in Your sight.
And for those who have done wrong, bring genuine conviction, honest confession, repentance, and accountability.
Break the power of deception.
Destroy the excuses that keep people enslaved to sin.
Lead us all to the cross, where Your holiness and mercy meet.
Lord Jesus, teach us to love as You loved.
Not selfishly.
Not possessively.
Not with hidden agendas.
But with truth, purity, sacrifice, and grace.
May our homes be places of safety.
May our churches be places where evil is confronted and the wounded are cared for.
May our friendships lead us closer to You.
And may our lives testify that Your Gospel truly transforms hearts.
In the mighty name of Jesus Christ,
Amen.
And remember this, long after you close this page:
The wrong friend may help you open a door that destroys a life. The right friend will love you enough to stop you before you reach for the handle.
